Two-particle correlations have shown modification to the away-side shape in central Au+Au collisions relative to $pp$, d+Au and peripheral Au+Au collisions. Different scenarios can explain this modification including: large angle gluon radiation, jets deflected by transverse flow, path length dependent energy loss, Cerenkov gluon radiation of fast moving particles, and conical flow generated by hydrodynamic Mach-cone shock-waves. Three-particle correlations have the power to distinguish the scenarios with conical emission, conical flow and Cerenkov radiation, from other scenarios. In addition, the dependence of the observed shapes on the $p_T$ of the associated particles can be used to distinguish conical emission from a sonic boom (Mach-cone) and from QCD-Cerenkov radiation. We present results from STAR on 3-particle azimuthal correlations for a high $p_T$ trigger particle with two softer particles. Results are shown for $pp$, d+Au and high statistics Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$=200 GeV. An important aspect of the analysis is the subtraction of combinatorial backgrounds. Systematic uncertainties due to this subtraction and the flow harmonics v2 and v4 are investigated in detail. The implications of the results for the presence or absence of conical flow from Mach-cones are discussed.

outputs.L1:
Two-particle correlations have revealed modifications to the away-side correlation shape in central Au+Au collisions relative to those observed in $pp$, d+Au, and peripheral Au+Au collisions. Several scenarios have been proposed to explain this modification, including large-angle gluon radiation, jet deflection by transverse flow, path-length-dependent energy loss, Cerenkov gluon radiation from fast-moving particles, and conical flow generated by hydrodynamic Mach-cone shock waves.

Three-particle correlations provide a powerful means of distinguishing scenarios involving conical emission—such as conical flow and Cerenkov radiation—from other mechanisms. In addition, the dependence of the observed correlation shapes on the transverse momentum, $p_T$, of the associated particles can be used to differentiate conical emission arising from a sonic boom (Mach cone) from that produced by QCD-Cerenkov radiation.

We present STAR results on three-particle azimuthal correlations involving a high-$p_T$ trigger particle and two lower-$p_T$ associated particles. Results are shown for $pp$, d+Au, and high-statistics Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. A critical aspect of the analysis is the subtraction of combinatorial backgrounds. Systematic uncertainties associated with this subtraction, as well as with the flow harmonics $v_2$ and $v_4$, are investigated in detail. The implications of these results for the presence or absence of conical flow from Mach cones are discussed.

In central Au+Au collisions, two-particle correlation measurements reveal that the away-side structure differs from what is observed in $pp$, d+Au, and peripheral Au+Au interactions. Several mechanisms have been proposed to account for this change, such as gluon radiation at large angles, jet deflection caused by transverse flow, energy loss that depends on the traversed path length, Cerenkov gluon emission by rapidly moving particles, and conical flow produced through hydrodynamic Mach-cone shock waves.

Three-particle correlation studies can help separate scenarios involving conical emission—such as conical flow and Cerenkov radiation—from alternative explanations. Furthermore, examining how the measured correlation patterns vary with the transverse momentum, $p_T$, of the associated particles provides a way to discriminate between conical emission from a sonic-boom-like Mach cone and emission arising from QCD-Cerenkov radiation.

We report STAR measurements of three-particle azimuthal correlations involving a high-$p_T$ trigger particle and two lower-$p_T$ associated particles. The results include $pp$, d+Au, and high-statistics Au+Au collision data at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. A key component of the analysis is the removal of combinatorial background contributions. The systematic uncertainties connected with this background subtraction, as well as those associated with the flow harmonics $v_2$ and $v_4$, are examined carefully. The consequences of these findings for determining whether Mach-cone-induced conical flow is present are also considered.
outputs.L3:
Two-particle correlation measurements have shown that the away-side jet structure is significantly modified in central Au+Au collisions when compared with pp, d+Au, and peripheral Au+Au collisions. In elementary or small-system collisions, the away-side correlation is typically dominated by a relatively narrow peak near an azimuthal angle difference of \(\Delta\phi \approx \pi\), corresponding to back-to-back jet production. In central heavy-ion collisions, however, this away-side peak can become broadened, suppressed, or even split into a double-peak structure. Such changes indicate that the recoiling parton interacts strongly with the hot and dense medium produced in the collision.

Several physical mechanisms have been proposed to explain this modification of the away-side correlation. Medium-induced gluon radiation may redistribute the lost parton energy over a broad angular region. Jet deflection by transverse collective flow could shift the apparent direction of the away-side jet. Path-length-dependent parton energy loss may bias the observed correlations toward particular geometrical configurations in the medium. Other explanations involve more exotic collective or coherent phenomena, such as Cerenkov gluon radiation, in which a fast parton emits gluons at a characteristic angle while traversing the medium, or Mach-cone shock waves, in which energy deposited by a supersonic parton generates a conical pattern of emitted particles.

Three-particle correlation measurements provide a more differential tool for distinguishing among these scenarios. While two-particle correlations reveal that the away-side structure is modified, they do not uniquely identify the underlying mechanism. By studying the angular correlations among one high-\(p_T\) trigger particle and two associated particles, three-particle correlations can determine whether the away-side yield is distributed in a way consistent with conical emission. In a conical emission scenario, such as conical flow from a Mach cone or Cerenkov gluon radiation, the two associated particles may appear symmetrically displaced from \(\Delta\phi=\pi\), producing characteristic off-diagonal structures in the three-particle correlation function. In contrast, mechanisms such as simple jet broadening or deflection may produce different correlation patterns.

The transverse momentum dependence of the associated particles provides an additional means of separating competing interpretations. In Mach-cone emission, the cone angle is expected to be largely determined by the speed of sound in the medium and therefore should be relatively insensitive to the transverse momentum of the associated particles. By contrast, in QCD-Cerenkov radiation, the emission angle can depend on the momentum of the radiated gluons, leading to a stronger dependence of the observed correlation shape on associated-particle \(p_T\). Measuring how the away-side structure evolves with associated-particle transverse momentum can therefore help discriminate between Mach-cone shock-wave emission and Cerenkov-like gluon radiation.

In this context, STAR presents measurements of three-particle azimuthal correlations in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at a center-of-mass energy of \(\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200\) GeV. The comparison among these collision systems allows medium-induced effects in central Au+Au collisions to be separated from baseline jet correlations and cold nuclear matter effects. A key part of the analysis is the careful treatment of combinatorial backgrounds, which arise from random combinations of particles unrelated to the same hard scattering. In heavy-ion collisions, these backgrounds are further complicated by collective flow correlations, such as elliptic flow, that can mimic or distort jet-like structures. STAR therefore includes a detailed assessment of flow-related systematic uncertainties to ensure that the extracted three-particle correlation signals reflect genuine medium-modified jet phenomena. These measurements provide important constraints on the mechanisms responsible for the modified away-side correlations observed in high-energy heavy-ion collisions.
outputs.L4:
Three-particle azimuthal correlations provide a powerful tool for studying the modification of jets in the hot and dense medium created in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. In central Au+Au collisions at RHIC energies, two-particle correlations have shown that the away-side jet, instead of appearing as a single peak opposite the trigger particle at Δφ ≈ π as in pp or d+Au collisions, can become broadened, flattened, or even split into a double-peak structure. Such behavior suggests that the recoil parton may be strongly modified by interactions with the medium. Several physical mechanisms have been proposed to explain this modified away-side shape, including conical emission from Mach-cone shock waves, Cerenkov-like gluon radiation, large-angle gluon radiation, jet deflection by collective flow, and path-length-dependent energy loss.

To distinguish among these possibilities, STAR has measured three-particle azimuthal correlations in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV. In this method, a high-pT trigger particle is selected as a proxy for a jet fragment, and the azimuthal angles of two associated particles are measured relative to the trigger direction. The resulting correlation function contains information not only about the average away-side structure, but also about whether the associated particles are correlated with each other in a pattern consistent with cone-like emission. For example, if the away-side particles are emitted on a cone around the direction of the recoil parton, the three-particle correlation should show characteristic off-diagonal structures in the two-dimensional distribution of Δφ1 and Δφ2. These structures differ from those expected from simple jet broadening, random deflection of the recoil jet, or independent particle emission modulated only by collective flow.

A major challenge in this analysis is the accurate subtraction of combinatorial background. In heavy-ion collisions, the large number of produced particles creates substantial background correlations that are not directly related to jets. These backgrounds are strongly influenced by anisotropic collective flow, especially elliptic flow v2 and higher harmonics such as v4. STAR therefore evaluated the background using detailed flow measurements and included systematic uncertainties associated with the reaction-plane dependence, the magnitude of v2, and assumptions about the relation between v4 and v2. Both hard–soft and soft–soft background contributions were considered, and the uncertainties from flow harmonics were propagated into the final three-particle correlation distributions.

The comparison among pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions is essential. In pp and d+Au collisions, where no large hot medium is expected, the three-particle correlations are dominated by ordinary jet fragmentation. The away-side structure is consistent with a relatively narrow recoil jet near Δφ ≈ π. In contrast, central Au+Au collisions show a significantly modified away-side correlation. The three-particle correlation surface contains structures away from the diagonal, indicating that the two associated particles can appear at different azimuthal angles relative to the trigger. Such off-diagonal features are qualitatively consistent with conical emission from the away-side parton.

The extracted cone angle in central Au+Au collisions is found to be roughly constant over the measured associated-particle transverse-momentum range and does not show a strong dependence on centrality within uncertainties. This behavior is one of the observations that may favor a collective medium response, such as Mach-cone-like conical flow, over mechanisms in which the emission angle would be expected to depend strongly on particle momentum. However, the interpretation is not unique. Other effects, including fluctuating initial geometry, triangular flow, jet deflection, and path-length-dependent jet-medium interactions, can also contribute to or mimic similar away-side structures.

Within the STAR analysis, the observed three-particle correlation patterns in central Au+Au collisions are compatible with a conical emission scenario, but they do not provide definitive proof of Mach-cone shock-wave formation. The results do not rule out conical flow from Mach cones, but the sizable systematic uncertainties from background subtraction and flow harmonics limit the strength of the conclusion. In particular, the precise magnitude and shape of the off-diagonal correlation structures depend on the treatment of v2 and v4 backgrounds. Therefore, while the measurements provide important evidence for strong jet-medium coupling and a nontrivial medium response to energetic partons, they cannot uniquely distinguish Mach-cone flow from all other possible mechanisms.

Overall, STAR’s three-particle azimuthal correlation measurements demonstrate that the away-side jet in central Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV is substantially modified relative to pp and d+Au reference systems. The data reveal correlation structures consistent with cone-like emission, suggesting that the recoiling parton deposits energy and momentum into the surrounding medium. However, because of background and flow-related uncertainties, the results should be interpreted as supporting, rather than conclusively proving, the presence of Mach-cone-induced conical flow.
outputs.L5:
Two different Cerenkov detectors can be used to study particles moving at extremely high speeds. Cerenkov radiation appears when a charged particle travels through a medium faster than light can travel in that same medium. This does not mean the particle is faster than light in a vacuum; instead, it is faster than the reduced speed of light inside materials such as water, glass, or gas.

The first type of Cerenkov detector may use water as its medium. When fast particles pass through the water, they produce a faint blue glow. Scientists can observe this light to identify the presence and direction of the particles. Large water-based Cerenkov detectors are often used in neutrino experiments and cosmic-ray research.

The second type may use gas or aerogel. These different materials allow researchers to detect particles with specific speeds and energies. By comparing the light produced in two different Cerenkov systems, scientists can learn more about the particle’s velocity, mass, and identity.

In this way, two different Cerenkov techniques can provide valuable information about invisible particles and high-energy events in physics.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a STAR physics conference talk on three-particle azimuthal correlations in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV, focusing on Mach-cone/conical flow interpretations and background subtraction systematics.
counterfactuals.output:
**Three-Particle Azimuthal Correlations in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au Collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV from STAR**

Measurements of di-hadron azimuthal correlations at RHIC have revealed strong modification of the away-side jet-like correlation in central Au+Au collisions, including broadening and possible double-peak structures, suggestive of medium response to energetic partons. Proposed interpretations include Mach-cone shock waves, conical Čerenkov-like gluon radiation, deflected jets, and path-length–dependent jet quenching. To further constrain these scenarios, three-particle azimuthal correlations provide additional topological information beyond two-particle measurements, enabling separation of conical emission patterns from simple away-side broadening or event-by-event jet deflection.

We present STAR measurements of three-particle azimuthal correlations in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV. Correlations are constructed with a high-pT trigger particle and two lower-pT associated particles, and are studied as a function of collision system and centrality. The pp and d+Au data provide baseline measurements of vacuum jet fragmentation and cold nuclear matter effects, while Au+Au collisions probe the response of the hot, dense medium created in heavy-ion interactions. In central Au+Au events, the away-side three-particle correlation exhibits structures consistent with off-diagonal peaks expected from conical emission, in addition to diagonal contributions associated with dijet fragmentation, broadening, or deflection.

A central focus of this talk is the treatment of combinatorial backgrounds and the associated systematic uncertainties. Backgrounds from random particle combinations, elliptic and higher-order harmonic flow correlations, and trigger-associated correlations coupled to the underlying event are evaluated and subtracted using mixed-event techniques and measured anisotropic flow coefficients. The sensitivity of the extracted signal to assumptions on v₂, v₄, background normalization, and factorization is examined. We discuss how these uncertainties affect the interpretation of the observed three-particle structures and the extent to which they support Mach-cone or more general conical-flow scenarios.

These measurements provide important constraints on the mechanism of away-side modification in heavy-ion collisions and on the coupling of hard-scattered partons to the QCD medium.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the motivation and main analysis issues for using 3-particle correlations to distinguish away-side jet modification mechanisms in central Au+Au collisions at RHIC.
counterfactuals.output:
In central Au+Au collisions at RHIC, two-particle azimuthal correlations with a high-\(p_T\) trigger showed a strongly modified away side: instead of a single recoil peak at \(\Delta\phi \approx \pi\), the associated yield often appeared broadened or double-peaked around \(\pi \pm 1\) rad. This was interpreted as possible evidence for strong parton energy loss and medium response, but two-particle correlations alone cannot uniquely identify the mechanism.

## Motivation for 3-particle correlations

Three-particle correlations use one high-\(p_T\) trigger particle and two lower-\(p_T\) associated particles, studying the distribution in

\[
(\Delta\phi_1,\Delta\phi_2)
=
(\phi_{a1}-\phi_{\rm trig},\phi_{a2}-\phi_{\rm trig}).
\]

The goal is to distinguish different away-side jet-modification scenarios that can look similar in two-particle correlations.

### 1. Conical emission / Mach-cone-like response

If the quenched away-side parton excites a conical shock wave or other cone-like medium response, associated particles are emitted around the away-side direction at angles

\[
\Delta\phi \approx \pi \pm \theta .
\]

In a 3-particle correlation, this should produce not only “diagonal” structures where both associated particles are on the same side of the cone,

\[
(\pi+\theta,\pi+\theta), \quad (\pi-\theta,\pi-\theta),
\]

but also “off-diagonal” structures where one particle is emitted on each side,

\[
(\pi+\theta,\pi-\theta), \quad (\pi-\theta,\pi+\theta).
\]

The off-diagonal peaks are a key signature of conical emission.

### 2. Deflected jets / bent recoil partons

If the away-side jet is simply deflected event-by-event by flow or scattering in the medium, then both associated particles from the recoil jet tend to appear at the same displaced angle. This gives primarily diagonal peaks in the 3-particle correlation, but little or no off-diagonal structure.

Thus, 3-particle correlations can test whether the away-side double peak is due to a cone-like topology or to an event-by-event displaced single jet.

### 3. Other scenarios

They can also help constrain alternatives such as large-angle gluon radiation, Cherenkov-like radiation, punch-through jets, path-length-dependent energy loss, or correlations arising from collective flow fluctuations.

## Main analysis issues

The measurement is difficult because the true jet-related 3-particle signal is small compared with the large combinatorial background in central Au+Au collisions.

### 1. Large combinatorial background

Central Au+Au events have very high multiplicity. Most trigger-associated-associated triplets are not genuine jet triplets but random combinations of particles from the bulk medium. The measured distribution contains contributions such as:

- one trigger plus two uncorrelated background particles,
- one genuine jet-associated particle plus one random background particle,
- correlations among background particles themselves,
- near-side and away-side jet fragments.

Careful background construction and subtraction are essential.

### 2. Flow background subtraction

The bulk medium has strong collective anisotropic flow, especially elliptic flow \(v_2\), and also higher harmonics such as \(v_3\), \(v_4\), etc. These produce long-range azimuthal correlations unrelated to jets. If not subtracted accurately, flow can create or distort apparent away-side structures.

For 3-particle correlations, the flow background is more complicated than in two-particle analyses because one must account for correlated modulation of all three particles relative to the reaction plane or event planes.

Uncertainties in \(v_n\), flow fluctuations, nonflow contributions, and event-plane correlations are major systematic issues.

### 3. Background normalization

Methods such as ZYAM-like assumptions are often used to fix the level of the combinatorial background. Small errors in the background normalization can strongly affect the extracted away-side shape, especially because the jet signal is a small difference between two large numbers.

### 4. Acceptance and detector effects

The raw 3-particle distribution must be corrected for detector acceptance, pair efficiency, limited pseudorapidity coverage, track merging, and two-track resolution effects. Mixed-event techniques are typically used, but residual acceptance effects can influence the 2D correlation surface.

### 5. Distinguishing genuine 3-particle structure from projected two-particle effects

Some apparent 3-particle features can arise from combinations of independent two-particle correlations rather than a genuine three-body correlation. The analysis must separate true three-particle jet-like correlations from products of lower-order correlations.

### 6. Trigger bias and kinematic dependence

A high-\(p_T\) trigger in central Au+Au is biased toward jets produced near the surface and traveling outward. The away-side parton then traverses a long path through the medium. The observed structure depends strongly on trigger \(p_T\), associated-particle \(p_T\), centrality, and pseudorapidity acceptance.

### 7. Ambiguity of interpretation

Even if off-diagonal strength is observed, interpreting it uniquely as a Mach cone is difficult. Medium flow, fluctuating initial geometry, triangular flow, multiple scattering, broadened jets, and other collective effects can also contribute. Therefore, 3-particle correlations provide stronger topological information than two-particle correlations, but they do not by themselves give an unambiguous microscopic mechanism.

## Summary

The motivation for 3-particle correlations is that they provide a two-dimensional angular topology of the modified away-side jet. A conical emission pattern should generate both diagonal and off-diagonal peaks at \(\pi \pm \theta\), while a deflected jet should mainly generate diagonal structures. This makes 3-particle correlations a powerful tool for distinguishing possible mechanisms behind the away-side double peak observed in central Au+Au collisions at RHIC.

The main challenges are the huge combinatorial background, accurate subtraction of anisotropic flow, normalization uncertainties, detector acceptance corrections, separation of genuine three-particle correlations from lower-order correlations, and the non-unique interpretation of the remaining signal.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: High-\(p_T\)-triggered three-particle azimuthal correlations, constructed with two softer associated particles, provide a sensitive probe of the medium response to energetic partons in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Unlike two-particle correlations, these measurements retain information on the relative angular structure of the away-side yield and can help distinguish competing mechanisms for the observed broadening or splitting of recoil-jet correlations. Large-angle gluon radiation and deflected jets are expected to produce characteristic off-axis correlation patterns, while Cherenkov gluon radiation and Mach-cone shock waves can generate conical emission with correlated yields at symmetric angles about the recoil direction. By examining the joint distribution of the two associated particles relative to the trigger, one can separate diagonal structures, indicative of event-by-event deflection, from off-diagonal components consistent with conical emission. Such three-particle correlation studies therefore constrain the dynamics of parton energy loss, jet–medium coupling, and collective excitation of the quark–gluon plasma.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a heavy-ion physics abstract describing STAR results on three-particle azimuthal correlations in pp, d+Au, and high-statistics Au+Au at 200 GeV, with emphasis on v2/v4 flow background uncertainties and implications for conical emission.
counterfactuals.output:
We report STAR measurements of three-particle azimuthal correlations in pp, d+Au, and high-statistics Au+Au collisions at \(\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200\) GeV. The analysis uses a high-\(p_T\) trigger particle and two associated charged particles to study the structure of jet-like correlations and medium-modified away-side emission. Measurements in pp and d+Au provide reference distributions dominated by jet fragmentation, resonance decays, and momentum conservation, while Au+Au collisions exhibit substantial modifications relative to these baseline systems.

A central challenge in extracting the genuine three-particle correlation signal in Au+Au is the subtraction of combinatorial backgrounds modulated by anisotropic flow. In particular, uncertainties in the elliptic-flow coefficient \(v_2\), its event-by-event fluctuations, and the fourth harmonic \(v_4\), including possible correlations between the trigger and associated particles, lead to significant systematic uncertainties in the residual correlation structure. We examine the sensitivity of the extracted signal to different assumptions for \(v_2\) and \(v_4\), including reaction-plane-dependent background estimates and variations between two- and multi-particle flow measurements.

After flow-background subtraction, the three-particle correlation surfaces in central Au+Au collisions show broad away-side structures inconsistent with a simple superposition of vacuum-like back-to-back jets. The observed off-diagonal and diagonal correlation strength is qualitatively consistent with scenarios involving conical emission or deflected jet propagation in the strongly interacting medium. However, the magnitude and detailed topology of the extracted signal depend strongly on the assumed flow background, especially the \(v_2\) and \(v_4\) components. These results demonstrate that three-particle correlations provide a powerful constraint on the origin of the away-side broadening, but also show that quantitative claims of conical emission require precise control of harmonic-flow backgrounds and their associated systematic uncertainties.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a conference proceeding abstract explaining how associated-particle pT dependence in three-particle correlations can discriminate Mach-cone sonic booms from QCD-Cherenkov radiation in RHIC Au+Au collisions.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Three-particle azimuthal correlations provide a differential tool for identifying the origin of the double-peaked away-side structure observed in high-\(p_T\) triggered Au+Au collisions at RHIC. In particular, the dependence of the associated-particle transverse momentum, \(p_T^{\rm assoc}\), offers a discriminant between two classes of conical-emission scenarios: Mach-cone shock waves generated by supersonic parton energy loss in the quark-gluon medium, and QCD-Cherenkov gluon radiation arising from an in-medium chromodielectric response.

For a Mach-cone interpretation, the cone angle is governed primarily by the medium speed of sound, \(\cos\theta_M = c_s/v_{\rm jet}\), and is therefore expected to be approximately independent of the momentum of the emitted associated hadrons, aside from broadening due to flow, thermal smearing, and fragmentation. Thus, in three-particle correlations, the off-diagonal structures corresponding to correlated away-side pairs should appear at a nearly fixed angular separation from the trigger direction over a broad range of \(p_T^{\rm assoc}\).

In contrast, QCD-Cherenkov radiation predicts an emission angle controlled by the gluon dispersion relation in the medium, \(\cos\theta_C = 1/[n(\omega)\beta]\), where the effective chromorefractive index \(n(\omega)\) depends on the radiated gluon energy. After hadronization, this implies a measurable dependence of the conical angle on associated-particle momentum: lower- and higher-\(p_T^{\rm assoc}\) particles should populate different away-side angular separations if the Cherenkov mechanism dominates.

We discuss how three-particle correlation measurements in central Au+Au collisions can separate genuine conical emission from deflected jets and background correlations by examining the two-dimensional distribution in \((\Delta\phi_1,\Delta\phi_2)\), after subtraction of combinatorial and collective-flow contributions. A momentum-independent cone angle would favor a hydrodynamic Mach-cone response to localized jet energy deposition, providing sensitivity to the medium equation of state through \(c_s\). Conversely, a systematic narrowing or widening of the cone with \(p_T^{\rm assoc}\) would support a dispersive QCD-Cherenkov radiation picture. The associated-\(p_T\) dependence of three-particle correlations therefore constitutes a critical observable for distinguishing sonic-boom–like medium response from coherent gluon radiation in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
